overview.title: Model size flattens, data grows: Figure 16.8
overview.main_topic: Recent LLM scaling trends: parameter counts levelling off while pretraining dataset sizes keep rising; continued investment in scale
overview.central_idea: Once it became clear that GPT-3-era models were too big for their compute (a smaller model trained on more data does better), parameter counts trended flatter while training data grew by orders of magnitude. Scaling compute still improves next-token prediction with no plateau in sight, so companies keep investing billions.
overview.importance: Figure 16.8 condenses seven years of LLM history into two log-scale plots and gives the quantitative backdrop for the chapter's closing discussion: data limits, deployment cost and reinforcement learning (p.530).
learning_objectives: Explain why recent model sizes have flattened while data sizes have increased.
Read log-scale scatter plots of parameters and tokens over time.
Identify roughly where key models (GPT-1 to Llama 3) sit in parameters and pretraining tokens.
State the authors' view that scaling compute still improves next-token prediction without a visible asymptote.
Explain why proprietary models such as GPT-4 and Gemini are missing from the figure.
prerequisites: Fixed compute budget: data vs model size trade-off (p.528)

summary:
**Finishing the compute argument (from p.528).** With a fixed pretraining budget you must split floating-point operations between **model size** and **amount of data**. Research showed GPT-3 (175B parameters) was too large for its budget: a smaller model trained on more data would give **better model performance**. "So recently, **model sizes have trended flatter while data sizes have trended up**."

**Scaling is not over.** The authors stress that this does *not* mean scaling will stop. More computing power **does** generally lead to better LLM performance, and there is **no sign yet of an asymptote** where next-token prediction performance levels off. Companies keep investing **billions of dollars** in scaling LLMs to see what new capabilities emerge.

**Figure 16.8** shows major LLMs released from 2018 to 2025. Both panels have log-scale y-axes.
- **Top, parameters (billions):** GPT-1 (~0.1B, 2018), BERT and RoBERTa (~0.3B), GPT-2 (~1.5B, 2019), Turing-NLG (~17B, 2020), GPT-3 (~175B, 2020), Gopher (~280B, late 2021), BLOOM (~176B, 2022), Llama (~65B) and Llama 2 (~70B, 2023), Gemma (~7B, 2024), Gemma 2 (~27B, 2024), Llama 3 (~405B, 2024). After GPT-3, the points no longer climb steadily: many important models are *smaller*.
- **Bottom, pretraining tokens (billions):** a near-straight line on the log scale, from a few billion tokens (GPT-1) to about 300B (GPT-3, Gopher), about 1.4T (Llama), 2T (Llama 2), about 6T (Gemma) and about 13-15T (Gemma 2, Llama 3), roughly 1,000x growth in five years.

The caption notes that many recent **proprietary** LLMs (GPT-4, Gemini) are not included because their details have not been disclosed. The figure's BERT/RoBERTa token values look anomalously low (see review flags).

paragraphs.excerpt: better model performance. So recently, model sizes have trended flatter while data sizes have
paragraphs.what_it_says: (Completing p.528's sentence: a smaller model trained on more data would have led to) better model performance. So recently, model sizes have trended flatter while data sizes have trended up.
paragraphs.what_it_means: For a fixed compute budget C, training cost grows with both parameter count N and token count D. If a model is 'too big', spending the same compute on a smaller model with more data lowers the final loss. Beyond the book: this is the 'compute-optimal' or Chinchilla result (Hoffmann et al., 2022), which suggested roughly 20 training tokens per parameter, far more than GPT-3's roughly 1.7. Since then, labs have gone well beyond even that ratio, because a smaller model is also cheaper to serve (p.530).
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It explains the shape of both panels of Figure 16.8.

paragraphs.excerpt: This doesn't mean that scaling will stop—more computing power does generally lead to better
paragraphs.what_it_says: Scaling will not stop: more compute generally improves LLM performance, and no asymptote in next-token prediction performance has appeared yet. Companies keep investing billions to scale LLMs and see what new capabilities emerge.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The claim is about **next-token prediction loss**: empirically it keeps falling smoothly (roughly as a power law) as compute grows. Note the careful scope. A lower next-token loss is not the same as general intelligence. Chapter 19 (p.595) argues that scaling-law benchmarks are largely memorization tests and that scale alone isn't all you need. 'See what new capabilities emerge' reflects that some abilities seem to appear only at larger scales, which is part of what motivates the investment.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: It balances the previous sentence: the trade-off changed *how* to scale (more data per parameter), not *whether* to scale.

concepts.name: Scaling (compute, parameters, data)
concepts.definition: The empirical observation that LLM performance (next-token prediction) improves predictably as compute, model size and data grow.
concepts.intuition: More resources reliably buy lower loss, and there is a best way to split them between model size and data.
concepts.technical: Beyond the book: training compute is roughly C ≈ 6ND flops (N parameters, D tokens); for a fixed C, the loss-minimizing N and D both grow roughly as the square root of C.
concepts.significance: It explains why models stopped getting bigger and started reading more data.
concepts.example: GPT-3: 175B params on about 300B tokens; Llama 3 405B on about 15T tokens.
concepts.misconception: 'Bigger model' and 'more scaling' are not the same thing; scaling data can matter as much or more.

concepts.name: Compute-optimal trade-off
concepts.definition: For a fixed pretraining budget, choosing model size and data size to get the best performance.
concepts.intuition: A fixed amount of flops can make a big model read a little or a smaller model read a lot.
concepts.technical: The book (p.528) says GPT-3 was too big for its budget; a smaller model with more data would have performed better.
concepts.significance: It is why model sizes 'trended flatter while data sizes trended up'.
concepts.example: Gemma 7B trained on about 6T tokens: about 860 tokens per parameter.
concepts.misconception: Compute-optimal for training is not the same as optimal for deployment; for serving, even smaller over-trained models can be preferable (p.530).

concepts.name: Large language model scale
concepts.definition: LLMs use billions of parameters and are trained on trillions of tokens.
concepts.intuition: Figure 16.8 is a map of how big 'large' has become.
concepts.technical: From GPT-1 (~117M params) to Llama 3 (405B); data from billions to about 15T tokens.
concepts.significance: It sets the scale context for running and fine-tuning such models (memory, cost).
concepts.example: The Gemma models used in this chapter (1B and 4B) are small by these standards.
concepts.misconception: The largest public models are not necessarily the best; data and post-training matter greatly.

deeper.title: Tokens per parameter across Figure 16.8 (approximate)
deeper.body:
Using approximate published values:

| Model | Params | Tokens | Tokens/param |
|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-3 (2020) | 175B | ~300B | ~1.7 |
| Gopher (2021) | 280B | ~300B | ~1.1 |
| Llama (2023) | 65B | ~1.4T | ~22 |
| Llama 2 (2023) | 70B | ~2T | ~29 |
| Gemma (2024) | 7B | ~6T | ~860 |
| Gemma 2 (2024) | 27B | ~13T | ~480 |
| Llama 3 (2024) | 405B | ~15T | ~37 |

The jump from about 1-2 tokens per parameter to tens or hundreds is the 'flatter sizes, more data' trend in numbers. Beyond the book: about 20 tokens per parameter is the commonly cited compute-optimal ratio (Chinchilla, 2022). Small models like Gemma go far beyond it because they are cheaper to serve.

deeper.title: Reading log-scale axes
deeper.body:
1. Each major gridline (10^0, 10^1, 10^2...) is a factor of 10.
2. A straight upward line on a log axis means **exponential** growth. The bottom panel is roughly straight: tokens grew about 10x every 1-1.5 years.
3. Equal vertical distances are equal *ratios*: GPT-2 to GPT-3 in the top panel is about two gridlines, about 100x (1.5B to 175B).
4. The top panel's lack of an upward trend after 2020 shows parameter counts staying within about 7B-405B, while the bottom panel keeps climbing.

deeper.title: Analogy: study time vs brain size
deeper.body: With a fixed tuition budget, you could hire a brilliant tutor for a few hours or a good tutor for many weeks. GPT-3 was the brilliant tutor for too few hours. Recent models choose a good-enough tutor and much more study time, and because the tutor is cheaper to keep around, it is also cheaper to consult afterwards (deployment).

misconceptions.claim: Model sizes flattening means scaling has stopped working.
misconceptions.correction: The authors say more compute still generally improves LLM performance, with no asymptote yet; the gains are now pursued mainly with more data.

misconceptions.claim: The newest models are always the biggest.
misconceptions.correction: Figure 16.8 shows 2024 models ranging from about 7B (Gemma) to 405B (Llama 3), many smaller than 2021's Gopher (280B).

misconceptions.claim: Figure 16.8 shows the absolute frontier of LLM size.
misconceptions.correction: Proprietary models like GPT-4 and Gemini are excluded because their details are undisclosed.

misconceptions.claim: Lower next-token loss from scaling means models become generally intelligent.
misconceptions.correction: The page's claim concerns next-token prediction performance; chapter 19 (p.595) argues scale alone isn't all you need.

takeaways: Since GPT-3, model sizes have trended flatter while pretraining data has grown by orders of magnitude.
A smaller model trained on more data can beat a larger, undertrained one at the same compute.
More compute still improves next-token prediction, with no visible asymptote, so investment in scale continues.
In Figure 16.8, parameters jump about 1,000x from 2018 to 2020 and then scatter (about 7B-405B), while tokens rise steadily to about 15T.
Proprietary frontier models (GPT-4, Gemini) are absent from the figure because their details are undisclosed.

questions.question: Why have LLM parameter counts trended flatter recently, according to the book?
options: For a fixed compute budget, a smaller model trained on more data performs better than a larger undertrained one
questions.answer: For a fixed compute budget, a smaller model trained on more data performs better than a larger undertrained one
questions.explanation: This is the argument completed at the top of the page (from p.528). Hardware is not cited as the cause, larger models are not always worse (Llama 3 is 405B), and regulation is not mentioned.

questions.question: Does the book say scaling LLMs has stopped paying off? Quote or paraphrase its claim.
questions.answer: No. More computing power does generally lead to better LLM performance, and there are no signs yet of an asymptote in next-token prediction performance.
questions.explanation: p529_e04 explicitly rejects the idea that scaling will stop.

questions.question: Using Figure 16.8's approximate values, compute tokens per parameter for GPT-3 (175B params, about 300B tokens) and Llama 2 (70B params, about 2T tokens).
questions.answer: GPT-3: about 1.7 tokens per parameter; Llama 2: about 29 tokens per parameter.
questions.explanation: 300/175 ≈ 1.7; 2000/70 ≈ 28.6. The roughly 17x increase quantifies 'data sizes have trended up' relative to model size.

questions.question: On a log-scale axis, what does a roughly straight upward trend over time (as in the bottom panel) indicate?
questions.answer: Exponential growth: the quantity multiplies by a roughly constant factor per unit of time.
questions.explanation: On log axes, equal vertical distances are equal ratios, so a straight line means a constant growth rate.

questions.question: Why are GPT-4 and Gemini not shown in Figure 16.8?
options: They are smaller than the plotted models
Their model details have not been disclosed
questions.answer: Their model details have not been disclosed
questions.explanation: The caption says so directly. Their size is unknown, so we cannot say they are smaller. They are Transformer-based, and both were released after 2018.

questions.question: Which model in the top panel is the largest, and which 2024 model is the smallest?
questions.answer: Llama 3 (about 405B) is the largest; Gemma (about 7B) is the smallest 2024 model shown.
questions.explanation: Read from the top panel of Figure 16.8.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why the Gemma models used in this chapter (1B and 4B) can be strong despite being far smaller than GPT-3?
questions.answer: They are trained on vastly more data per parameter (trillions of tokens), and they benefit from extensive post-training (SFT, RLHF, distillation; p.521).
questions.explanation: This combines the data-scaling trend in Figure 16.8 with the post-training discussion on p.521.
